{
  "hypothesis": "Predicted that expanding time horizons at work would reduce the preference for emotionally meaningful work activities (helping colleagues) compared to future-oriented work activities, thereby eliminating age-related differences in these preferences.",
  "design": "between",
  "manipulation_or_predictor": "Experimental manipulation of occupational time horizons (unspecified, expanded, or limited) and participant age.",
  "outcome_measure": "Forced-choice preference among three work-related activities: helping a colleague (emotionally meaningful), working on a career-advancing project (future-oriented), or working on a project leading the company in a new direction (future-oriented).",
  "population_and_setting": "Employed adults recruited via KnowledgePanel of GfK Research.",
  "sample_size_total": 555,
  "recruitment_and_incentive": "Recruited from a larger study about decisions and regret; no specific incentive mentioned for this task.",
  "analysis_plan": "Logistic regression to test the effect of time horizon condition on the likelihood of choosing to help a colleague over future-oriented activities, including age and the interaction between age and condition.",
  "preregistered_or_confirmatory": "not stated",
  "other_methods_notes": "The study used an adapted version of the Fredrickson and Carstensen (1990) social partner paradigm. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: unspecified, expanded (told they would stay with the company longer), or limited (told their contract would expire soon)."
}
